content: An oogonium (plural: oogonia) is an immature ovum, also known as a female gametogonium. These cells are formed in large numbers through mitosis during early fetal development, originating from primordial germ cells. Primordial germ cells are present in the fetus between weeks 4 and 8 of gestation. Oogonia themselves are present in the fetus from approximately week 5 to week 30 of development. In addition to their role in human reproduction, oogonia are also reproductive structures in certain thallophytes, where they typically appear as rounded cells or sacs containing one or more oospheres. Once primordial germ cells reach the ovary, they differentiate into oogonia. During the sixth week of fetal development, these cells migrate from the yolk sac to the genital ridge, which is located on the posterior abdominal wall and will later develop into the gonads (ovaries in this case). Oogonia proliferate through mitosis, but some of them transition into primary oocytes. These primary oocytes initiate meiosis, but the process is arrested in prophase I. It is important to note that this transition into primary oocytes and the arrest in prophase I are completed before birth, which contrasts with spermatogenesis in males. Primary oocytes remain in this arrested state from approximately week 10 of fetal development until menopause, which typically occurs around the age of 53. Oogamy, which may also be spelled oögamy with a diaeresis or umlaut, refers to a form of sexual reproduction. In this process, the female oogonium usually enlarges and develops into a single ovum. In contrast, the male reproductive structure (antheridium) typically produces numerous flagellated cells, except in the Rhodophyta (red algae), which lack flagella. There is no evidence to suggest that red algae ever possessed flagella or cilia, and it is hypothesized that they may represent some of the most primitive eukaryotes. Oogonia are also found in fungi, where they serve as reproductive structures.
